title: Tesla Q1 2026 Cash Flow
subtitle: Net income vs operating cash flow - where the gap comes from
openingQuestion: Why can a company post positive net income and still show weak operating cash flow?
openingOptions: Because the revenue has not been collected in cash yet
Because the accounting ratios are wrong
Because there is no tax charge
explanation: Revenue and profit can be recognised before the cash actually arrives, especially when receivables and working capital are climbing. At fast-growing businesses that gap can persist for several quarters in a row while the company keeps scaling up its operations.

realWorldExample.company: Three questions to ask when a growth business burns cash
realWorldExample.description: Negative operating cash flow at a business that is expanding fast is not by itself a bad signal, but it always raises three questions. First, where is the cash locked up - receivables, inventory, or capital spending? Second, will that turn into revenue in later periods, or does it just keep piling up? Third, what is funding the company through this stretch - cash on hand, new borrowing, or a share issue that dilutes existing owners? A business that can answer all three and shows improvement quarter by quarter is investing; a business that cannot is burning cash.

quiz.question: When is OCF typically weaker than net income?
options: When the dividend payout rises during the period
When the gross margin improves versus last quarter
When borrowing rates fall and interest expense drops
When receivables rise sharply during the period
quiz.explanation: Working capital expanding traps cash inside the business: the sale is booked as revenue but the money is still sitting in receivables. Dividends are a financing outflow and never touch operating cash flow at all. A better gross margin lifts profit and cash together, so it opens no gap between them. Cheaper borrowing cuts interest expense, which also helps profit and cash in the same direction.

quiz.question: A fast-growing company reports positive net income for several quarters but persistently negative OCF because CapEx and working capital are climbing. Is that automatically a bad sign?
options: Not automatically bad - it depends on funding and returns
Not important - net income is the only figure to watch
Yes, this is always a bad sign and you should sell the stock now
Only bad if the firm is US-listed and reports under US GAAP
quiz.explanation: Plenty of fast-growing businesses, Tesla during its expansion phase among them, run negative OCF for perfectly sound reasons because they are investing heavily for the future. What matters is whether the company has the funding to keep going and whether that spending earns a decent ROIC over the long run, rather than the sign in front of the number on its own.

quiz.question: What separates 'investing for growth' from 'burning cash' when operating cash flow is negative?
options: Whether the firm reports positive accounting profit that period
Whether the locked-up cash turns into revenue in later periods
The absolute size of the negative cash flow in the latest quarter
Whether the company has already listed on a stock exchange
quiz.explanation: Both cases produce negative cash flow today, so nothing in the current period tells them apart. Only what happens in the periods that follow does, which is why you track the trend rather than judge from a single quarter. Accounting profit, headline size and listing status are all present at the same moment in both cases and therefore carry no information here.

quiz.question: Why look at operating cash flow on a rolling four-quarter basis rather than quarter by quarter?
options: Because quarterly reports are unaudited and cannot be trusted
Because companies disclose cash flow once per financial year
Because working capital swings by season, so one quarter misleads
Because a four-quarter total always comes out cash-flow positive
quiz.explanation: Many industries have a pronounced peak season: inventory builds ahead of it and drains afterwards. Adding four quarters together strips out that noise and shows the underlying trend. Quarterly reports are reviewed and published, cash flow is disclosed every quarter, and a rolling total is perfectly capable of coming out negative.

quiz.question: How do you tell negative cash flow from expansion apart from negative cash flow caused by a weak business model?
options: Check whether revenue is growing faster than the industry
Check whether the annual report discloses an expansion plan
Check whether net profit for the period is positive after all costs
Check whether the negative sits in operating or in investing
quiz.explanation: Buying a plant shows up in investing cash flow and is a choice that can be stopped. Negative operating cash flow is different: the act of selling itself consumes cash, so the more you sell the faster you run dry - and that is the signal that the model does not yet work.

keyTakeaways: Net income is no substitute for cash flow
Working capital and CapEx are the two biggest sources of the gap
Reading a report means reading both profit and cash

summary.keyIdea: Net income is no substitute for cash flow
summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: working capital and CapEx are the two biggest sources of the gap
summary.action: Reading a report means reading both profit and cash

sections.text: A company posts positive net income several quarters running and its operating cash flow is still weak - a situation you meet constantly at fast-growing businesses.
Revenue booked first, cash arrives later

Revenue and profit can be recognised before the cash actually arrives, particularly when receivables and working capital grow as fast as the business does. That is not automatically a bad sign - the question is whether the company is investing in genuine future growth, and whether it has enough funding (raised or borrowed) to sustain itself through this stretch of negative OCF.

items: A sharp rise in receivables is the most common reason OCF lags net income
Negative OCF at a fast-growing business can be perfectly sound if the spending is well directed and the funding is there
Net income does not remove the need to track working capital and CapEx as well

sections.text: Four figures to track together across quarters

items: Receivables growth against revenue growth - receivables running ahead for several quarters in a row signals credit terms being loosened.
Days inventory outstanding - a rising number means goods are turning over more slowly, even while revenue keeps climbing.
Rolling four-quarter operating cash flow - smooths the seasonal effect and shows the real trend more clearly than any single quarter.
How the shortfall is funded - read the financing section to see whether the company is borrowing more or issuing shares.

left.label: Investing for growth
left.text: Cash is locked into inventory and fixed assets that serve new capacity; revenue in later quarters rises to match; operating cash flow improves steadily as that capacity comes into use.

right.label: Burning cash
right.text: Cash is locked mainly into receivables that are hard to collect and inventory that moves slowly; revenue does not rise to match; operating cash flow goes deeper into the red each year and fresh capital has to be raised continuously to cover it.

sections.label: Look at the rolling total, not one quarter
sections.text: Working capital swings hard with the seasons, so a single quarter of negative cash flow says almost nothing. Four quarters added together, compared with the same period last year, is the shortest view wide enough to draw a conclusion about the trend.

lines: Do not jump to a negative conclusion just because OCF is negative.
The better question is: does the business have the funding to get through this phase, and will that spending create value over the long run?

practicePrompt.question: When you analyse Tesla's Q1 2026 accounts, why can operating cash flow (OCF) diverge so widely from net income?
options: Depreciation, working capital swings and stock-based comp
The accountants made an error adding and subtracting figures
Because Tesla does not pay its electricity and water bills
Because net income is always exactly equal to operating cash flow
practicePrompt.explanation: Accrual net income differs from OCF because of non-cash charges (depreciation, SBC) and because working capital ties up cash that profit has already recognised.
